BREAKING: Global debt jumped by more than +$10 trillion in H1 2026, to a record $365 trillion.

Emerging-market debt drove the increase, rising +$6.5 trillion, to a record $110 trillion, with most of the surge coming from governments and non-financial companies.

Excluding China, emerging-market and developing-economy debt soared to a record $38 trillion.

Global debt now stands at ~310% of global GDP, although the ratio has fallen -25 percentage points from its early-2021 peak, largely because inflation has boosted nominal GDP rather than because of deleveraging.

Meanwhile, developed economies paid more than $3.3 trillion in interest on marketable government debt over the last year, exceeding estimated global spending on AI at $2.6 trillion, defense at $3.1 trillion, and clean energy at $2.3 trillion.

This comes as annual government interest payments across the G7 alone surged +85% YoY.

The global debt crisis is in uncharted territory.

I think people are underselling RWA perps by calling them “24/7 stocks.”

The pre-IPO angle here is way more interesting.

@CoinMarketCap has already tracked $6.4B in pre-IPO perp volume across names like SpaceX, OpenAI, and Anthropic.

That means there's a lot of interest in trading them.

Btw, trading these pre-IPO perps doesn’t mean you’re buying shares. You’re actually trading the market-implied valuation of these companies before they go public.

Being able to trade stocks on a Sunday is a nice advantage. But that mostly extends access to markets retail already has.

And pre-IPO perps open exposure to companies like OpenAI or SpaceX that most retail investors otherwise can’t trade before they go public.

Not bad.

I’ve read the entire “Confidential Transfers” thesis from @SuiNetwork.

Here’s my honest take:

1. Public-by-Default has tradeoffs

Blockchains are transparent.

It's fine for traders and DeFi users who want to verify activity, but for businesses, that same transparency can expose a lot of information that they'd normally keep internal.

Things like:

→ Payroll amounts
→ Treasury movements
→ Supplier payments
→ Revenue flows

They can reveal quite a bit about the company and how it operates.

Businesses need the benefits of public settlement without exposing every financial detail.

2. Selective privacy > full anonymity

I agree with Sui’s approach here to keep balances and payment amounts private without making the whole system anonymous.

Businesses still need auditors, compliance teams, and issuers to access certain information when needed.

So the data stays private by default, with access still available to authorized parties.

That feels much closer to how businesses already handle financial privacy.

3. Confidential finance works better as a stack

A private transfer can hide the payment itself, but businesses also need to keep the systems around that payment private.

That includes things like payroll software, finance records, and rules for who can access certain information.

In my understanding, Sui is pairing Confidential Transfers with:

→ Seal for controlling who can access sensitive data
→ Nautilus for processing sensitive data privately
→ Gasless transfers for simpler stablecoin payment flows

This approach makes privacy a part of the whole flow, not just the transfer.

A much better setup in my opinion.

My takeaway:

Crypto-native users like you and me are already used to these defaults in crypto. It's a feature, not a bug after all these years.

I'm talking about things like public balances, visible transaction history, or separate gas tokens.

But they're not really optimal for businesses.

Finance moving onchain needs a middle ground, where it has verifiable settlement, more control over what becomes public, and fewer DeFi steps around the payment itself.

So I think Sui is getting that balance right with its confidential finance stack.

Better defaults make onchain finance easier to use, especially for businesses.

And it's a way for the crypto space to scale exponentially.

Disclosure: I’m a $SUI holder.

if you’re a trader you have no idea how op adding episodic memory is to your agent.

what is this and why is it over powered?

the best traders in the world will attribute success to journalling their trades.

well that same journalling will let you create episodic memory which may well turn you from a shit trader who never learns his lessons into best trader you can become.

when you journal you should be recording:

> what did i expect the market to do?
> what actually happened?
> what was my directional bias?
> what setup did i take?
> why did i enter?
> where was my invalidation?
> how much did i risk?
> how did i size / scale the trade?
> what was my emotional state?
> did i feel fomo, fear, greed, boredom or complacency?
> did i actually follow my plan?
> why did i exit?
> what was the result?
> what did i do well?
> what did i fuck up?
> what lesson should i remember next time?

this will let you create episodic memory.

you can now tell your agent in the future:

> find every trade where i used this setup before
> show me how often it worked
> show me my average return
> show me the market conditions where it worked best
> show me the conditions where it failed
> show me the mistakes i normally make with this setup
> show me how my emotional state affected my execution
> show me similar losing trades and what went wrong
> show me similar winning trades and what i did right

and now when you go to make a trade and you journal:

> current market conditions
> directional bias
> setup
> entry
> invalidation
> risk
> sizing
> catalyst
> expected outcome
> emotional state

your agent can compare it against every similar trade you have taken before.

it can tell you the exact success rate you had with this exact setup.

it can tell you your average R.

it can tell you when the setup normally works.

it can tell you when it normally fails.

it can tell you the mistakes you repeatedly make.

it can even tell you:

“you have taken this setup 14 times before.

9 were winners.

your average return was +1.7R.

but when you entered before confirmation you lost 4 out of 5 times.”

now your agent is not just analysing the market.

it is analysing your own trading history.

every trade becomes another memory.

every mistake becomes something it can retrieve.

every successful setup becomes something it can compare against.

the more journalling the more episodic memory. the more episodic memory the more wins.

okay, I’m actually going to share a @bot with you guys soon so you can steal this.

The current barrier to greater AI diffusion isn’t model capability. In my eyes, the barrier is three things (in order):

1. Most people don’t understand what AI can do
2. They need to fundamentally think differently about their life and work
3. Human preference. Even if AI can do the thing, people still want to do it (like shopping)

Each layer is a more rigid barrier. First, someone must be motivated to understand. 

Then, they have to build a habit of flipping their thinking to a more AI-forward way. They need to consider how they would deconstruct and assign out work as if they were a manager. They need to understand abstract capabilities and apply them to their own use cases, or understand what previous use cases were uneconomical that are now available. 

Then they need to want to assign that task out to AI in the first place

All of this leads me to believe that we are still incredibly early. It will take 3-5 years for the middle of the curve to even understand today’s AI capabilities and change their mindset to put this technology to work on their behalf. And by then we will be much more advanced. 

The technological capability isn’t the blocker. It’s our understanding, creativity, and preferences that will determine the pace of diffusion

2. They need to fundamentally think differently about their life and work
3. Human preference. Even if AI can do the thing, people still want to do it (like shopping)

Each layer is a more rigid barrier. First, someone must be motivated to understand. 

Then, they have to build a habit of flipping their thinking to a more AI-forward way. They need to consider how they would deconstruct and assign out work as if they were a manager. They need to understand abstract capabilities and apply them to their own use cases, or understand what previous use cases were uneconomical that are now available. 

Then they need to want to assign that task out to AI in the first place

All of this leads me to believe that we are still incredibly early. It will take 3-5 years for the middle of the curve to even understand today’s AI capabilities and change their mindset to put this technology to work on their behalf. And by then we will be much more advanced. 

The technological capability isn’t the blocker. It’s our understanding, creativity, and preferences that will determine the pace of diffusion

tweets.text:
Most agent failures today are really memory failures.

The model is usually capable enough. What’s missing is the graph around you: who your wife is, who your closest friends are, how you know someone, what you last discussed, which channel you use with them, recurring context, preferences, commitments, etc.

Most systems build memory slowly through nightly “dreaming” over your conversations. That creates a nasty cold-start problem: the agent needs days or weeks of interaction before it actually knows you well...

And even then, many systems store memory as a flat pile of facts instead of maintaining a proper person-level memory layer. Muse does this better: you can effectively end up with wife.md, best_friend.md, coworker_x.md aka persistent context for each important person.

You can bootstrap this yourself today. Give a local agent access to your iMessage, WhatsApp, email and calendar history on your computer and ask it to:

"resolve identities across channels
cluster messages/events by person
infer relationships and recurring topics
rank people by recency + frequency + reciprocity
generate one Markdown memory file per person, with timestamps and evidence"

It may take hours over a large corpus, but you skip the cold start entirely and end up with hundreds of high-quality person-specific memories on day one. That makes every downstream agent dramatically less context-blind. 

Then you can give the memories files to your preferred agent. @nikunj gave me the idea yesterday to look more at my local data (he has his own killer agent system)
